title: Religio Medici
alternative_titles: Religio Medici: Its Author's Name is Thomas Browne
description: Sir Thomas Browne's meditative confession of faith, written privately in the 1630s and pirated in 1642 before Browne issued his own authorised text in 1643; it is the founding work of English introspective prose.
plot_or_argument: In two parts Browne sets out his religious faith and his moral philosophy: the first defends his adherence to the Church of England against the charges of atheism and scepticism, the second explores charity and the duty to one's neighbour.
narrative_structure: Two parts of continuous meditative prose without formal division into chapters in the first edition.
meter_and_prosody: A richly Latinate, periodic prose with a strong personal cadence; Browne's style became the model of English 'character' writing.
historical_context: Written while Browne was practising medicine, probably in the late 1630s; circulated in manuscript and printed without his consent in 1642, then authorised in 1643 with his own preface.
literary_significance: The most influential work of English prose of the seventeenth century after the Authorised Bible; it created the genre of the personal religious meditation in prose and influenced Montaigne's English readers, Coleridge, Lamb, and Virginia Woolf.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Browne; he authorised the 1643 edition after the pirated 1642 printing.
bibliographical_notes: First (unauthorised) edition 1642; authorised edition 1643. Standard edition: The Major Works of Sir Thomas Browne (C. A. Patrides, ed., Penguin Classics, 1977); The Works of Sir Thomas Browne (L. C. Martin, ed., 1964-6).

title: Pseudodoxia Epidemica; or, Enquiries into Very Many Received Tenets
description: Browne's encyclopaedic survey of popular errors, in seven books examining and correcting the received beliefs of his time about natural history, medicine, geography, history, and Scripture.
plot_or_argument: Book I analyses the causes of error; books II-IV treat errors concerning animals, plants, minerals, and man; books V-VII treat errors of history, chronology, and Scripture.
narrative_structure: Seven books of learned enquiry organised by subject, each entry stating the received opinion and Browne's correction.
meter_and_prosody: Learned, allusive prose of great compression; the work went through five editions in Browne's lifetime.
historical_context: Published in 1646, in the midst of the civil wars; it belongs to the new empirical spirit that would found the Royal Society, though Browne's method is as much scholarly as experimental.
literary_significance: The greatest English work of popular scepticism and one of the most important documents of seventeenth-century intellectual life; it influenced Baconian empiricism and the Royal Society's programme.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1646; five editions to 1672. Standard edition: Pseudodoxia Epidemica (Robin Robbins, ed., Oxford University Press, 1981), 2 vols.

title: Hydriotaphia; or, Urn-Burial
description: Browne's treatise on the burial of the dead, occasioned by the discovery of Roman urns in Norfolk, which moves from antiquarian description to the great meditation on mortality and oblivion that is its famous second half.
plot_or_argument: Chapters I-III survey the burial customs of the ancient world; chapter IV reflects on the vanity of funerary monuments; chapter V, the peroration, meditates on the certainty of oblivion and the Christian hope of resurrection.
narrative_structure: Five chapters of increasing rhetorical intensity, ending in the celebrated chapter V.
meter_and_prosody: The most magnificent prose of the seventeenth century; the closing paragraphs of chapter V are among the most quoted passages in English.
historical_context: Published in 1658, in the same year as The Garden of Cyrus and the death of Cromwell; it was written during the Commonwealth when Browne was living quietly at Norwich.
literary_significance: The supreme English meditation on death and oblivion; it has influenced writers from Johnson and De Quincey to W. G. Sebald, and its phrases ('that vulgar arithmetic of antiquity', 'to be ignorant of evil') are part of the language.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1658, bound with The Garden of Cyrus. Standard edition: The Major Works of Sir Thomas Browne (C. A. Patrides, ed., Penguin Classics, 1977).

title: The Garden of Cyrus
alternative_titles: The Garden of Cyrus: Discourse on the Quincunx
description: The companion piece to Hydriotaphia, a learned and increasingly mystical discourse on the quincunx — the five-point arrangement — as it appears in the gardens of Cyrus, in nature, and in art, and as an emblem of cosmic order.
plot_or_argument: Browne traces the quincunx from the Hanging Gardens of Cyrus through Roman military formations, botanical patterns, and the arrangement of the stars, arguing that the figure reveals a divine geometrical order in creation.
narrative_structure: Five chapters of accumulating pattern and digression, ending in a nocturnal vision.
meter_and_prosody: Dense, incantatory prose; the concluding 'night-piece' is famous for its drowsy cadences.
historical_context: Published in 1658 together with Hydriotaphia and dedicated to Nicholas Bacon.
literary_significance: A unique experiment in emblematic natural philosophy and one of the strangest and most beautiful works of English prose; it has been a touchstone for critics interested in the seventeenth-century imagination.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1658. Standard edition: The Major Works of Sir Thomas Browne (C. A. Patrides, ed., Penguin Classics, 1977).

title: Christian Morals
description: Browne's posthumously published manual of Christian conduct in three parts, a series of terse aphorisms and exhortations on the duties of the Christian life.
plot_or_argument: Part I treats the grounds of Christian virtue; part II treats duties to God, self, and neighbour; part III treats the hope of immortality and the contempt of the world.
narrative_structure: Three parts of numbered aphoristic chapters.
meter_and_prosody: Compressed, gnomic prose.
historical_context: Written in Browne's later years and left in manuscript at his death in 1682; first printed in 1716 with a life by John Whitefoot.
literary_significance: An important late work that shows Browne's moral philosophy in aphoristic form and completed the eighteenth-century view of him as a Christian moralist.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1716. Standard edition: The Works of Sir Thomas Browne (L. C. Martin, ed., 1964-6).

title: The Compleat Angler; or, The Contemplative Man's Recreation
description: Izaak Walton's pastoral dialogue on fishing, in which the angler Piscator instructs Venator, combining practical lore on the taking of fish with songs, poems, and reflections on the contemplative life; the fifth edition of 1676 added Charles Cotton's second part.
plot_or_argument: Over five days of dialogue, Piscator teaches Venator and Auceps the arts of angling and defends the quiet life of the angler against the pursuits of the hunter and the falconer.
narrative_structure: A pastoral dialogue in five chapters or days, interspersed with songs, verse quotations, and digressions.
principal_characters: Piscator (the angler); Venator (the huntsman); Auceps (the falconer); Peter Manwood; Piscator's scholar
meter_and_prosody: Gentle, conversational prose with interpolated songs and verses.
historical_context: First published in 1653, in the Commonwealth, when Walton had withdrawn from public life; revised and expanded in five editions to 1676, when Charles Cotton's part on fly-fishing was added.
literary_significance: One of the most reprinted books in English (over 400 editions), a founding text of the English pastoral tradition, and the standard expression of the ideal of quiet country retirement.
attribution_notes: Parts I-III by Walton; the 1676 edition adds Part II by Charles Cotton (not in this database), who is named on the title page.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1653; fifth edition 1676 with Cotton. Standard edition: The Compleat Angler (Marjorie Swann, ed., Oxford University Press, 2014).

title: Lives (Walton)
alternative_titles: The Lives of Doctor John Donne, Sir Henry Wotton, Mr Richard Hooker, Doctor George Herbert, and Doctor Robert Sanderson
description: Walton's five biographies of Donne (1640), Wotton (1651), Hooker (1665), Herbert (1670), and Sanderson (1678), collected in 1670 and revised until his death in 1683; they created the modern English literary biography and the hagiographic ideal of the Anglican divine.
plot_or_argument: Each life presents its subject as a model of Christian virtue: Donne the penitent preacher, Wotton the courtier-diplomat, Hooker the learned divine, Herbert the country parson, Sanderson the casuist.
narrative_structure: Five separate lives, each with a portrait, letters, and verses.
principal_characters: John Donne; Sir Henry Wotton; Richard Hooker; George Herbert; Robert Sanderson
meter_and_prosody: A deceptively simple, warm prose of anecdote and character.
historical_context: Written across the civil wars, Commonwealth, and Restoration; the Life of Donne was based on Walton's personal knowledge and on Donne's own papers.
literary_significance: The Lives established Walton as the founder of English biographical prose and shaped the Anglican devotional ideal of the holy life; modern scholarship has shown their factual liberties, but their literary influence is immense.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Walton; the Life of Donne has been shown to borrow heavily from Donne's own writings and from earlier sources.
bibliographical_notes: Lives collected 1670; fifth edition 1675. Standard edition: The Lives of the eminent persons (A. H. Bullen, ed.); Izaak Walton's Lives (Oxford World's Classics).

title: The Rule and Exercises of Holy Living
description: Jeremy Taylor's devotional manual of the Christian life, written during the civil wars while Taylor was deprived of his living, and one of the most popular religious books of the seventeenth century.
plot_or_argument: Four chapters treat the universal instrument of holy living: the nature and measures of temperance, of justice, of the Christian religion, and of prayer, with directions for the practice of each virtue.
narrative_structure: Four books of systematic devotional instruction with prayers at the end of each.
meter_and_prosody: Oratorical, richly figurative prose of the Anglican baroque; Taylor was called 'the Shakespeare of the divines'.
historical_context: Published in 1650, after the execution of Charles I, when Taylor was living in retirement in Wales under the patronage of the Earl of Carbery.
literary_significance: With Holy Dying the most influential Anglican devotional work of the period; it defined the ideal of the holy life for generations and remains a classic of English prose.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1650. Standard edition: The Whole Works of the Right Rev. Jeremy Taylor (Reginald Heber, ed., 1822); Holy Living and Holy Dying (P. G. Stanwood, ed., Oxford University Press, 1989).

title: The Rule and Exercises of Holy Dying
description: The companion volume to Holy Living, a manual for the dying that instructs the Christian in the preparation for death, with famous meditations on the vanity of the world.
plot_or_argument: Four chapters treat the consideration of death, the temptations that beset the dying, the practice of patience and repentance, and the exercises and prayers for the dying.
narrative_structure: Four books of instruction with prayers.
meter_and_prosody: Baroque Anglican prose of great rhetorical power.
historical_context: Published in 1651, dedicated to the Countess of Carbery, whose death occasioned the book; it belongs to the long tradition of the ars moriendi.
literary_significance: One of the most widely read devotional works in English; it shaped the Protestant art of dying and influenced the elegiac and meditative literature of the period.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1651. Standard edition: Holy Living and Holy Dying (P. G. Stanwood, ed., OUP, 1989).

title: The Holy State and the Profane State
description: Thomas Fuller's most popular work, a book of 'characters' describing the ideal states of the church, the family, the court, and the commonwealth, followed by the contrary vices of the profane state.
plot_or_argument: The first part describes the good parson, the good husband, the good magistrate, the good soldier, and the like; the second part describes their profane opposites; the third part gives the history of the Church from the creation.
narrative_structure: A series of short character-pieces followed by a historical narrative.
principal_characters: the good parson; the good husband; the good magistrate; the good soldier; the good merchant; their profane opposites
meter_and_prosody: Fuller's characteristic pithy, epigrammatic, punning prose.
historical_context: Published in 1642, on the eve of the civil wars, and dedicated to the Lady Montagu; it was reprinted throughout the century.
literary_significance: The most influential English collection of characters after Earle and the principal model of the pithy, aphoristic prose style that Johnson imitated.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1642, Cambridge. Standard edition: The Holy State and the Profane State (Frank Livingstone Huntley, ed., 1938).

title: The History of the Worthies of England
description: Fuller's great county-by-county biographical and antiquarian survey of the notable men and women of England, with descriptions of each county's natural resources, wonders, and families; it was published posthumously in 1662.
plot_or_argument: Each county is treated in a uniform sequence: its natural commodities, manufactures, wonders, battles, families, and memorable persons, with biographical notices of its 'worthies'.
narrative_structure: An alphabetical arrangement by county with a general introduction.
meter_and_prosody: Fuller's characteristically digressive, witty, and compressed prose.
historical_context: Written during the Commonwealth and published in 1662, after Fuller's death in 1661; it is the first systematic topographical and biographical dictionary of England.
literary_significance: A foundational work of English local history and biography, and the source for countless later antiquarians; it remains in use as a biographical reference.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1662, London. Standard edition: The History of the Worthies of England (P. Austin Nuttall, ed., 1840), 3 vols.

title: Brief Lives
description: John Aubrey's vast collection of biographical memoranda on the notable men of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries — Bacon, Hobbes, Shakespeare, Donne, Milton, Harvey, and hundreds more — compiled as notes for Anthony Wood's Athenae Oxonienses and never published in his lifetime.
plot_or_argument: The entries are informal, gossipy, and anecdotal, recording physical appearance, habits, sayings, and eccentricities alongside dates and facts, in Aubrey's own hurried hand with gaps and marginal queries.
narrative_structure: An alphabetical collection of biographical memoranda, many incomplete, with Aubrey's characteristic asterisks and queries.
principal_characters: Thomas Hobbes; William Shakespeare; John Milton; Francis Bacon; John Donne; William Harvey; Sir Walter Raleigh
meter_and_prosody: Informal, hurried, anecdotal prose, often in note form.
historical_context: Compiled chiefly between 1669 and 1696, partly for Anthony Wood; the manuscripts passed to the Bodleian and were first printed in part in 1813.
literary_significance: The most vivid and most human biographical source for seventeenth-century England; Aubrey's method of personal recollection and physical detail anticipates modern biography, and the Lives have been continuously read since their publication.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Aubrey; the manuscripts are in his own hand.
bibliographical_notes: Manuscripts in the Bodleian Library; first printed in Letters Written by Eminent Persons (1813). Standard edition: Brief Lives, chiefly of Contemporaries, 1669-1696 (Andrew Clark, ed., Clarendon Press, 1898), 2 vols.

title: Letters from Dorothy Osborne to Sir William Temple
description: The seventy-seven surviving letters written by Dorothy Osborne to William Temple during their long courtship in 1652-4, in which she discusses her family's opposition to the match, the books she is reading, and the state of the country under the Commonwealth.
plot_or_argument: The letters trace the progress of the courtship against Osborne's brother's opposition and her own reluctance; they range freely over literature, gossip, politics, and the difficulty of a woman's position.
narrative_structure: A sequence of letters over about two years, with gaps.
principal_characters: Dorothy Osborne; Sir William Temple; Sir Peter Osborne; Osborne's brother Henry
meter_and_prosody: An easy, natural, unselfconscious prose that is the earliest great example of familiar English letter-writing.
historical_context: Written 1652-4, during the Commonwealth, when Osborne was confined at Chicksands and Temple was travelling; they married in 1654.
literary_significance: The finest English letters of the seventeenth century and a crucial document of women's writing; their spontaneous style was admired by Virginia Woolf and they are the standard by which later familiar letters are judged.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Osborne; the manuscripts were printed in 1847 from the family papers (first partly published in 1713).
bibliographical_notes: Manuscripts in the British Library; standard edition: The Letters of Dorothy Osborne to William Temple (E. A. B. Osborn, ed., 1928); Letters of Dorothy Osborne (Kenneth Parker, ed., Penguin Classics, 1988).

title: Observations upon the United Provinces of the Netherlands
description: Temple's political and social analysis of the Dutch Republic, written after his years as English ambassador at The Hague, and one of the most influential English works of political observation of the period.
plot_or_argument: Temple describes the constitution, government, religion, military strength, trade, and character of the United Provinces, and analyses why a small republic could rival the great monarchies of Europe.
narrative_structure: A series of short chapters on the several aspects of Dutch government and society.
meter_and_prosody: Clear, urbane prose in the new plain style.
historical_context: Written in 1672-3 during the Franco-Dutch War and published in 1673; Temple was a leading Whig diplomat and a patron of Swift.
literary_significance: A classic of early modern political analysis and a model of plain prose; it influenced Montesquieu's Spirit of the Laws and the English debate on republicanism.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1673. Standard edition: Observations upon the United Provinces of the Netherlands (G. W. Prothero, ed., Oxford University Press, 1932).

title: Of Ancient and Modern Learning
alternative_titles: Essay upon the Original and Nature of Poetry (included)
description: Temple's essay defending the ancients against the moderns, written in reply to Fontenelle and the French Académie, and containing the famous praise of the Epistles of Phalaris; it opened the English Quarrel of the Books.
plot_or_argument: Temple argues that the ancients surpassed the moderns in poetry, oratory, and philosophy, cites the Epistles of Phalaris as the oldest and best of the ancient letters, and dismisses modern learning as pedantic.
narrative_structure: A single continuous essay.
meter_and_prosody: Plain, urbane prose.
historical_context: Published in 1692 in Temple's Miscellanea; it provoked Wotton's Reflections upon Ancient and Modern Learning (1694) and Bentley's demonstration that the Epistles of Phalaris were a later forgery, in which the young Swift served as Temple's amanuensis.
literary_significance: The opening salvo of the English Battle of the Books, which Swift satirised in The Battle of the Books (1704); it is a key text in the history of the quarrel between the ancients and the moderns.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Miscellanea, the Second Part (1690) and Miscellanea III (1692). Standard edition: Five Miscellaneous Essays by Sir William Temple (Louis B. Wright, ed., 1963).

title: The Diary of Samuel Pepys
description: Pepys's private shorthand diary, kept from 1 January 1660 to 31 May 1669, the most detailed and most candid account of daily life in Restoration England ever written, recording the Restoration, the coronation, the Plague, and the Fire of London.
plot_or_argument: The diary records Pepys's work at the Navy Board, his amours, his household, the theatre, music, books, politics, and the great public events, with an unflinching self-portrait of ambition, curiosity, and pleasure.
narrative_structure: A daily entry over nine and a half years, interrupted only by illness and the strain of failing eyesight.
principal_characters: Samuel Pepys; Elizabeth Pepys; Sir William Coventry; the Duke of York; Deb Willet; Mary Knep; Nell Gwyn
meter_and_prosody: Lively, colloquial, and confidential prose, written in Thomas Shelton's tachygraphy (shorthand) and not intended for publication.
historical_context: Kept during Pepys's rise in the naval administration and during the two great catastrophes of the Restoration; the diaries passed to Magdalene College, Cambridge, and were first deciphered and published in 1825.
literary_significance: The greatest diary in the English language and the single most important source for the social, political, and cultural history of the 1660s; it invented the modern confessional journal and has never been out of print since 1825.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Pepys; the manuscripts are in his own shorthand and were deciphered by John Smith in 1819-22.
bibliographical_notes: First published (in part) 1825; standard edition: The Diary of Samuel Pepys (Robert Latham and William Matthews, eds., Bell & Hyman / University of California Press, 1970-83), 11 vols.

title: The Diary of John Evelyn
alternative_titles: Memoirs Illustrative of the Life and Writings of John Evelyn
description: Evelyn's diary, kept intermittently from 1641 until a few days before his death in 1706, recording his European travels, the courts of Charles II and James II, the founding of the Royal Society, and his gardens and experiments at Sayes Court.
plot_or_argument: The diary records Evelyn's journeys in France and Italy, his observations on art, architecture, science, and gardening, the Great Plague and Fire, and the religious and political events of the Restoration.
narrative_structure: A continuous daily and occasional journal over sixty-five years.
principal_characters: John Evelyn; Mary Evelyn; Charles II; Robert Boyle; Samuel Pepys; Christopher Wren; Margaret Blagge
meter_and_prosody: Learned, observational, and sometimes ornate prose, more formal than Pepys's.
historical_context: Kept from 1641 to 1706; the manuscripts remained in the family until publication in 1818.
literary_significance: The indispensable companion to Pepys's diary for the history of the Restoration; Evelyn's account of the Great Fire, of the Royal Society, and of English gardening are standard sources.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Evelyn; the manuscripts are in his own hand.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1818 (W. Bray, ed.). Standard edition: The Diary of John Evelyn (E. S. de Beer, ed., Clarendon Press, 1955), 6 vols.

title: Sylva; or, A Discourse of Forest-Trees and the Propagation of Timber
description: Evelyn's treatise on trees and timber, written at the request of the Royal Society and the first book it published, which urged the planting of oaks and other timber for the navy and became a classic of forestry.
plot_or_argument: Evelyn describes the principal forest trees of England, their uses, propagation, and management, and argues that the nation's naval strength depends on the systematic planting of timber.
narrative_structure: Four books, each treating a group of trees, with appended treatises on fruit trees and on the propagation of timber.
meter_and_prosody: Learned but readable prose, with verse quotations and classical allusion.
historical_context: Published in 1664 as the first book issued by the Royal Society; four editions appeared in Evelyn's lifetime.
literary_significance: The founding text of English forestry and an important document of the new scientific culture; its practical influence on tree-planting was immediate and long-lasting.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1664; fourth edition 1706. Standard edition: Sylva (Guy de la Bédoyère, ed., Boydell Press, 1999); Kalendarium Hortense in The Works of John Evelyn (William Bray, ed., 1906).

title: Memoirs of the Life of Colonel Hutchinson
alternative_titles: Memoirs of the Life of Colonel John Hutchinson
description: Lucy Hutchinson's biography of her husband, the regicide Colonel John Hutchinson, written in the 1670s as a vindication of his honour and of the parliamentary cause, and the most important work of prose by a woman of the seventeenth century.
plot_or_argument: The memoir narrates Hutchinson's life from his education at Nottingham through his service for Parliament in the civil wars, his governance of Nottingham Castle, his refusal to vote at the king's trial, his imprisonment after the Restoration, and his death at Sandown Castle in 1664.
narrative_structure: A continuous biographical narrative with digressions on Lucy's own life and on the politics of the period.
principal_characters: Colonel John Hutchinson; Lucy Hutchinson; Sir Allen Apsley; Colonel Thomas Hutchinson; Oliver Cromwell; Charles I
meter_and_prosody: A clear, vigorous, and emotionally restrained prose, with moments of great eloquence.
historical_context: Written in the 1670s for her children and not published until 1806; it is a rare first-hand account of the parliamentary side by a woman of the gentry.
literary_significance: A canonical work of women's writing and of Restoration literary history; it is the most important prose life of a parliamentarian and a central text in the study of seventeenth-century women's authorship.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Lucy Hutchinson; the manuscript is in her hand.
bibliographical_notes: First published 1806 (Julius Hutchinson, ed.). Standard edition: Memoirs of the Life of Colonel Hutchinson (N. H. Keeble, ed., Dent/Everyman, 1995); The Works of Lucy Hutchinson (David Norbrook, ed., Oxford University Press, 1999- ).

title: Order and Disorder; or, The World Made and Undone
description: Lucy Hutchinson's biblical epic on Genesis, of which only canto V was published in her lifetime and the complete text survives in manuscript; it is the first epic poem in English by a woman and a direct answer to Milton's Paradise Lost.
plot_or_argument: The poem retells the story of creation, the fall, and the expulsion, interpreting Genesis through a Calvinist theology and a republican politics that laments the Restoration of monarchy.
narrative_structure: Twenty cantos in heroic couplets, of which only canto V was printed in 1679.
principal_characters: Adam; Eve; God; Satan; the angels
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets in iambic pentameter.
historical_context: Written after the Restoration, when Hutchinson, a widow and a Puritan, was reflecting on the failure of the republican cause; it engages directly with Milton's epic.
literary_significance: The first English epic by a woman and an important early response to Paradise Lost; its republicanism and its female epic voice have made it a canonical text of seventeenth-century women's writing.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Lucy Hutchinson; the manuscript is in her hand and was first published complete in 2001.
bibliographical_notes: Canto V printed 1679; complete text in the Nottingham University Library manuscript. Standard edition: Order and Disorder (David Norbrook, ed., Blackwell, 2001).

title: Translation of Lucretius, De Rerum Natura (Hutchinson)
description: Lucy Hutchinson's complete verse translation of Lucretius's De Rerum Natura, the first ever into English, undertaken in the 1650s and dedicated to the Earl of Anglesey; she later wrote a preface condemning the Epicurean philosophy she had so brilliantly rendered.
plot_or_argument: The translation renders all six books of Lucretius's didactic epic on Epicurean physics, the nature of the soul, the origin of society, and the fear of death.
narrative_structure: Six books in heroic couplets, following Lucretius's own structure.
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets; Hutchinson's version is the first complete English Lucretius.
historical_context: Composed in the 1650s and revised up to the 1670s; the manuscript was dedicated to Arthur Annesley, Earl of Anglesey, and remained unpublished until 1996.
literary_significance: A landmark of Restoration translation and of women's classical learning; its preface is a striking document of a devout Puritan woman negotiating with Epicurean materialism.
attribution_notes: Attributed to Lucy Hutchinson; the manuscript is in her hand with her prefatory address to the Earl of Anglesey.
bibliographical_notes: Manuscript in the Bodleian and at Nottingham; standard edition: Lucy Hutchinson's Translation of Lucretius: De Rerum Natura (Hugh de Quehen, ed., University of Michigan Press, 1996).
